content.title: Identifying Independent and Dependent Variables
content.overview: In ACT Science, success depends on distinguishing between the factor a researcher manipulates and the outcome they measure. This lesson teaches the 'Change-to-Measure Mapping' strategy to correctly identify independent and dependent variables in experimental descriptions.
learning_objectives: Define independent and dependent variables in the context of a scientific experiment.
Identify the independent variable as the factor deliberately changed or assigned by the researcher.
Identify the dependent variable as the outcome or result that is measured or recorded.
Distinguish between manipulated variables and constants or controlled factors.

sections.title: The Core Definitions
sections.content: Every experiment seeks to understand a cause-and-effect relationship. The Independent Variable (IV) is the 'cause'—it is the factor the researcher intentionally changes, varies, or assigns across different groups or trials. The Dependent Variable (DV) is the 'effect'—it is the outcome, response, or measurement that the researcher records to see how it reacts to the changes in the IV.

sections.title: The Change-to-Measure Mapping Strategy
sections.content:
To identify variables quickly on the ACT, follow these three steps: 1. Find the Change: Look for the factor that is different between groups (e.g., different temperatures, different dosages). This is your Independent Variable. 2. Find the Measurement: Look for what the researcher recorded at the end of the trial (e.g., time, mass, height). This is your Dependent Variable. 3. Verify: Ensure the IV is the manipulation and the DV is the result.

![A flow chart showing the process of identifying variables: Change leads to Independent Variable, and Measure leads to Dependent Variable.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/599623c3-8852-4614-9c60-9cf4c689dff4-1786506615929-122.webp)

sections.title: Variables in Data Displays
sections.content: On the ACT Science section, variables are often organized visually. In a standard graph, the Independent Variable is typically plotted on the horizontal x-axis, while the Dependent Variable is plotted on the vertical y-axis. In a data table, the Independent Variable usually occupies the leftmost column, while the Dependent Variables (the results) occupy the columns to the right.

worked_examples.question: A scientist investigates how different concentrations of salt affect the boiling point of water. She prepares four beakers with 100 mL of water each, adding 0g, 5g, 10g, and 15g of salt respectively. She then heats the water and records the temperature at which each solution begins to boil. Identify the independent and dependent variables.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify what was deliberately changed. The scientist varied the amount of salt (0g, 5g, 10g, 15g). This is the Independent Variable. Step 2: Identify what was measured. The scientist recorded the boiling temperature. This is the Dependent Variable. Step 3: Final Answer. Independent Variable: Salt concentration; Dependent Variable: Boiling point temperature.

common_mistakes: Confusing constants with variables: Do not pick a factor that stayed the same (like the 100 mL of water) as a variable.
Reversing the relationship: Thinking the measured outcome is what the scientist changed.
Ignoring units: Failing to include the specific measurement (e.g., 'height in cm') which helps clarify the dependent variable.
exam_tips: Look for words like 'varied,' 'assigned,' or 'different' to spot the independent variable.
Look for words like 'recorded,' 'measured,' or 'observed' to spot the dependent variable.
If a question asks about the 'effect of X on Y,' X is almost always the independent variable and Y is the dependent variable.
content.recap: The independent variable is the factor you change; the dependent variable is the result you measure. Use the Change-to-Measure Mapping strategy to link the researcher's manipulation to the recorded outcome.

knowledge_claims.content: The independent variable is the factor that a researcher intentionally changes or assigns across different groups or trials in an experiment.
The dependent variable is the outcome or response that is measured or recorded to assess the effect of the independent variable.
To identify the independent variable, look for the factor that is varied or different between experimental groups.
To identify the dependent variable, look for the specific quantity or observation that the researcher records at the end of a trial.
In a standard scientific graph, the independent variable is typically represented on the x-axis (horizontal).
In a standard scientific graph, the dependent variable is typically represented on the y-axis (vertical).
In a data table, the independent variable is usually located in the leftmost column.
A common error is misidentifying a constant—a factor held the same across all groups—as the independent variable.
A valid check for the dependent variable is to ask if the value was 'measured' or 'observed' rather than 'chosen' by the researcher.
The independent variable acts as the 'cause' in a study, while the dependent variable acts as the 'effect'.
If an experiment tests the effect of light duration on plant growth, light duration is the independent variable and plant growth is the dependent variable.
Keywords such as 'varied,' 'different,' or 'adjusted' often signal the presence of the independent variable in a passage.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 2: Dissolving Effervescent Tablets
Students tested how water temperature affects the time required for identical effervescent tablets to stop producing visible bubbles. In Experiment 1, they used 200 mL of water at four temperatures and one whole tablet per trial. In Experiment 2, they repeated the test with crushed tablets while keeping the water volume and temperatures unchanged.

Which factor was held constant and therefore helped make treatment comparisons meaningful?
A) water temperature and tablet form
B) time until visible bubbling stopped
C) the conclusion written after the experiment
D) water volume and tablet composition

options.C: the conclusion written after the experiment

items.explanation: A controlled factor is kept the same across conditions so differences can be attributed more confidently.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 3: Paper Rotor Descent
A class built paper rotors with two folded blades. Experiment 1 compared blade lengths while rotor mass was held constant. Experiment 2 added paper clips to the medium-blade rotor. Students released each rotor from the same height indoors and recorded mean descent time.

Which factor was held constant and therefore helped make treatment comparisons meaningful?
A) blade length in Experiment 1 and added mass in Experiment 2
B) release height and paper type
C) mean descent time
D) the conclusion written after the experiment

options.A: blade length in Experiment 1 and added mass in Experiment 2
options.D: the conclusion written after the experiment

items.explanation: A controlled factor is kept the same across conditions so differences can be attributed more confidently.
